## Two truths and a lie

An AI told me three things about R, very confidently.

1. R starts counting at 1, not 0.
2. `mean(c(1, 2, NA))` returns `1.5`.
3. `c(1, "a", TRUE)` turns everything into text.

. . .

::: {.vote}
Vote with fingers (1, 2, 3): which one is the lie?
:::

## The lie was #2


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(10, 20, 30)[1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 10
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(c(1, 2, NA))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] NA
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
c(1, "a", TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "1"    "a"    "TRUE"
```


:::
:::


. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** A confident wrong answer looks exactly like a confident right one.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two truths and a lie: #2 is the lie (it returns NA). Don't explain NA yet, we come back to it in the essentials section.
:::

# Who's driving? {background-color="#f3f6ea"}

::: {.notes}
Time 0:08–0:20 · Framing + first live bug.
:::

## The new division of labor

**AI drives**: writes code fast

**You navigate**: choose the destination, read the map, check the route

. . .

Fast driving is great. Driving into a lake is not.

## What does a navigator do?

1. **Set the destination**: say clearly what you want
2. **Read the route**: understand the code
3. **Check the road**: run it, test it
4. **Make the call**: accept, fix, or reject

## Why learn R if AI writes it?

You can't catch a wrong turn on a map you can't read.

. . .

The scariest bugs don't crash. They run fine and give a believable answer.

## The Audit Loop

1. **Read** it
2. **Run** it
3. **Restate** it in plain English
4. **Refine** it or **Reject** it

. . .

::: {.vote}
Restate is the superpower. If you can't say what a line does, you can't vouch for it.
:::

## Bug Bounty rules

- Every bug you catch: **+1 point** for your team
- Explain *why* an AI would make that mistake: **+1 bonus**
- Bugs hide in code **and** in answers that look fine

::: {.notes}
Keep the tally visible. Call on a different team each round.
:::

## Case #0: the request

> "Show me the 5 highest-rated movies on IMDb."

The AI wrote:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  arrange(imdb_rating) |>
  select(title, imdb_rating) |>
  head(5)
```
:::


## Your turn: Restate it

With your partner, 60 seconds:

Say each line in plain English. Does it match the request?

::: {.vote}
Navigator speaks, driver listens. Then swap.
:::

## Run it


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  arrange(imdb_rating) |>
  select(title, imdb_rating) |>
  head(5)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   title             imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                   <dbl>
#> 1 Disaster Movie            1.9
#> 2 Epic Movie                2.3
#> 3 Battlefield Earth         2.4
#> 4 Viva Knievel!             2.7
#> 5 Doogal                    2.8
```


:::
:::


. . .

::: {.vote}
Does this answer the request? Hands up: yes / no
:::

::: {.notes}
No. `arrange()` sorts ascending by default, so these are the five WORST rated (Disaster Movie 1.9, Epic Movie 2.3, Battlefield Earth 2.4, Viva Knievel! 2.7, Doogal 2.8). No error, no warning. Fix later with `desc()`. Award points.
:::

## Why this one is sneaky

- No error
- No warning
- A clean table that looks right

. . .

**Errors are the friendly failures.**

## Functions

A function has a name and arguments in parentheses.

```{.r .cell-code}

```

```
#> [1] 3.14
```


:::
:::


## Vectors

A vector is a row of values of one type. `c()` combines.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
scores <- c(72, 88, 91, 65)
mean(scores)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 79
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
scores * 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 144 176 182 130
```


:::
:::

Predict:

```{.r .cell-code}
NA > 5

```

## Handling NA


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- c(4, 8, NA)
mean(x)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] NA
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 6
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
is.na(x)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE
```


:::
:::


. . .

::: {.bug}
`na.rm = TRUE` is a **decision**, not a fix. You chose to ignore the unknowns.
:::

::: {.notes}
Plant the seed: dropping missing values changes who is in your analysis. This returns in the WellSync cleaning sessions.
:::

# Verbs and the pipe {background-color="#f3f6ea"}

::: {.notes}
Time 0:45–0:70 · dplyr verbs, Bug Court, Movie Night.
:::

## Data wrangling is a sentence

"Take movies, **then** keep the dramas, **then** sort by rating, **then** show the top 3."

. . .

The pipe `|>` reads as **then**.

## Same thing, two ways


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
head(arrange(filter(movies, genre == "Drama"), imdb_rating), 3)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  filter(genre == "Drama") |>
  arrange(imdb_rating) |>
  head(3)
```
:::


## You'll see two pipes

`|>` is built into R.

`%>%` is the older tidyverse pipe. AI and old tutorials use both.

They behave the same for what we do.

::: {.notes}
In Positron the pipe shortcut is Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+M. A setting decides which pipe it inserts.
:::

## `select()`: choose columns


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  select(title, genre, runtime, imdb_rating)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 651 × 4
#>   title                genre  runtime imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                <chr>    <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown          Drama       80         5.5
#> 2 The Dish             Drama      101         7.3
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman  Comedy      84         7.6
#> 4 The Age of Innocence Drama      139         7.2
#> 5 Malevolence          Horror      90         5.1
#> # ℹ 646 more rows
```


:::
:::


## `filter()`: keep rows


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  select(title, genre, imdb_rating) |>
  filter(genre == "Drama")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 305 × 3
#>   title                genre imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                <chr>       <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown          Drama         5.5
#> 2 The Dish             Drama         7.3
#> 3 The Age of Innocence Drama         7.2
#> 4 Lady Jane            Drama         7.2
#> 5 Mad Dog Time         Drama         5.5
#> # ℹ 300 more rows
```


:::
:::


## Conditions you can use

- `==` equal, `!=` not equal
- `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`
- `%in%` is in this set
- `is.na()` is missing
- `,` or `&` means **and**; `|` means **or**

## `filter()` with two conditions


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  select(title, genre, imdb_rating) |>
  filter(genre == "Drama", imdb_rating > 8)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   title             genre imdb_rating
#>   <chr>             <chr>       <dbl>
#> 1 Warrior           Drama         8.2
#> 2 V for Vendetta    Drama         8.2
#> 3 The Help          Drama         8.1
#> 4 Good Will Hunting Drama         8.3
#> 5 The Prestige      Drama         8.5
#> # ℹ 3 more rows
```


:::
:::

How many rows do you get?

::: {.swap}
Columns to use: `mpaa_rating`, `runtime`.
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  filter(mpaa_rating == "R", runtime > 150) |>
  select(title, runtime, imdb_rating)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 3 Topsy-Turvy                154         7.4

```

## Bug Court is in session

Each case: the request, the AI's code, and your verdict.

**Guilty** = it's wrong. **Innocent** = it's fine.

Use the Audit Loop. Restate before you vote.

## Case #1: the request

> "Keep the Drama and Comedy movies."


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  filter(genre == c("Drama", "Comedy"))
```
:::


::: {.vote}
Restate it. Guilty or innocent?
:::

## Case #1: the evidence


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |> filter(genre == c("Drama", "Comedy")) |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 191
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |> filter(genre %in% c("Drama", "Comedy")) |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 392
```


:::
:::


. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** `==` lines the two names up with rows one by one, back and forth. In your own console R also prints a warning. **Warnings are clues.**
:::

::: {.notes}
Guilty. 191 vs 392 rows. The recycling makes row 1 compare to "Drama", row 2 to "Comedy", row 3 to "Drama", and so on. Tie back to Challenge 1.
:::

## Case #2: the request

> "Keep movies that have a DVD release year."


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  filter(dvd_rel_year != NA)
```
:::


::: {.vote}
Guilty or innocent?
:::

## Case #2: the evidence


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |> filter(dvd_rel_year != NA) |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |> filter(!is.na(dvd_rel_year)) |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 643
```


:::
:::


. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** Anything compared with `NA` is `NA`, and `filter()` drops those. Zero rows, no error.
:::

## Case #2b: where did it go?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(movies)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 651
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |> filter(runtime > 0) |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 650
```


:::
:::


. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** Every movie has a runtime above 0, yet one vanished: its runtime is `NA`. `filter()` **quietly drops** rows where the condition is `NA`.
:::

::: {.notes}
650 vs 651. This is the first appearance of "who disappears silently?" which becomes the cleaning impact audit in Lab 2.
:::

## Case #3: the request

> "How many documentaries are in the data?"


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  filter(genre == "Documentary") |>
  nrow()
```
:::


::: {.vote}
Guilty or innocent? Look closely at the column names first.
:::

## Case #3: the evidence


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |> filter(genre == "Documentary") |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 52
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |> filter(title_type == "Documentary") |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 55
```


:::

. . .

::: {.bug}
**Bug:** The code is fine. The **question** was ambiguous. Two columns, two answers (52 vs 55).
:::

::: {.notes}
Neither answer is wrong. The navigator's job is to specify which column, or ask the AI which one it used. Great Week-3 theme: a good spec removes ambiguity.
:::

## `arrange()`: sort rows

Now fix Case #0.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  arrange(desc(imdb_rating)) |>
  select(title, imdb_rating)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 651 × 2
#>   title                  imdb_rating
#>   <chr>                        <dbl>
#> 1 The Godfather, Part II         9  
#> 2 Promises                       8.5
#> 3 Django Unchained               8.5
#> 4 Memento                        8.5
#> 5 The Prestige                   8.5
#> # ℹ 646 more rows
```


:::
:::


## `mutate()`: make new columns


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
movies |>
  mutate(runtime_hrs = runtime / 60) |>
  select(title, runtime, runtime_hrs)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 651 × 3
#>   title                runtime runtime_hrs
#>   <chr>                  <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 Filly Brown               80        1.33
#> 2 The Dish                 101        1.68
#> 3 Waiting for Guffman       84        1.4 
#> 4 The Age of Innocence     139        2.32
#> 5 Malevolence               90        1.5 
#> # ℹ 646 more rows
```


:::
:::


## Four verbs, four jobs

- `select()` picks **columns**
- `filter()` keeps **rows**
- `arrange()` changes **order**
- `mutate()` makes **new columns**

# Movie Night {background-color="#f3f6ea"}

::: {.notes}
Time ~0:60–0:70. Teams of 3–4. Rounds 1–2 by hand (5 min), Round 3 with AI (5 min). If short on time, drop Round 2.
:::

## How Movie Night works

Rounds 1 and 2: **by hand**.

Round 3: **with your AI**, and you audit it.

- Correct answer: **+1**
- Each bug you catch in the AI's code: **+1**

## Round 1 (by hand)

Among **R-rated Feature Films** longer than **150 minutes**, which has the **highest IMDb rating**?

::: {.swap}
Columns: `mpaa_rating`, `title_type`, `runtime`, `imdb_rating`
:::

::: {.notes}
Answer: The Godfather, Part II (202 min, IMDb 9.0). Same six rows as Challenge 3: all six are Feature Films, so adding the title_type condition doesn't change the result. Good moment to point out that the extra condition is still the safer spec.
:::

## Round 2 (by hand)

Which **Documentary** (`title_type`) has the **lowest** `audience_score`?

::: {.notes}
Answer: Sea Monsters: A Prehistoric Adventure (68). Next are Blind Spot: Hitler's Secretary (70) and Kicking It (71). Watch for teams that use `genre == "Documentary"` instead: the question names title_type.
:::

## A good prompt is a spec

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
